name: Ammianus Marcellinus
label: Outside witness
knownFor: A soldier and historian, not of the church, whose Roman History tells of the deadly fight for the bishopric of Rome, the emperor Julian's dealings with the Christians, and the killing of Bishop George at Alexandria.
dates: 330 to 400 in John Rolfe's dates; Charles Duke Yonge says only that he lived nearly to the end of the fourth century. His history ends with the death of Valens in 378
place: A native of Antioch, as Yonge reads the history; he wrote at Rome

keyWorks.title: Roman History (Res Gestae)
keyWorks.about: thirty-one books from the accession of Nerva in 96 to the death of Valens in 378; Yonge says the first thirteen are lost

remembered: Edward Gibbon, quoted by Yonge, called him "an accurate and faithful guide, who has composed the history of his own times." Gibbon goes on to say he wrote without the prejudices that usually affect a contemporary.
John Rolfe, who translated Suetonius, says Tacitus "did not find a follower until the time of Ammianus Marcellinus."

Charles Joseph Hefele's History of the Councils cites "the heathen historian Ammianus Marcellinus" for the emperor Constantius II's efforts to win Rome's consent to the deposition of Athanasius of Alexandria.

uncertain: Little is known of him beyond what his own history shows, and even his religion is uncertain. Yonge reports that "the general belief is, that he adhered to the religion of the ancient Romans."
Professor Ramsay, quoted by Yonge, praises his honesty and good sense, but says he "did not entirely escape the contagion" of his age's belief in omens and oracles.

On Julian's attempt to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem, E. A. Abbott, quoted by Blomfield Jackson in his notes to Theodoret of Cyrus, judges Ammianus an impartial historian. Abbott still accepts only that the work "was generally believed" to have been stopped by a fiery sign. He thinks it "was probably stopped by a violent thunderstorm or thunderstorms."
On church matters he reports what was said. He writes that Athanasius was deposed partly because, "it was said", he had foretold the future from auguries and omens.
The passage on Damasus and Ursinus gives no year. Yonge's page heading places it in 367.
The Library holds Yonge's 1862 English translation, from an uncorrected scan, and no Latin text.
